Blud
BLUD
noun (Gen-Z slang)
From blood as a kinship word. In Black American speech from the 1960s, blood was a term of address for a fellow Black man (it was common among Black soldiers in Vietnam), and in some US cities it was later claimed as a gang greeting. In London the spelling and sound became blud in Multicultural London English (MLE), the youth dialect that grew from Caribbean, African, and Cockney roots in the 1990s–2000s and was spread by grime and UK rap. American Gen Z picked it up c. 2022–2023 through TikTok, especially in the mocking meme format "blud thinks he’s…"

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In current slang blud means bro or mate: "you alright, blud?" On American TikTok it is mostly used in the third person to mock someone’s overconfidence: "blud thinks he’s the main character." The word is older and weightier than its users know: it is blood, the kinship of shared birth. The Christian observation: Scripture says both things the word implies, and then says something better. All men are already kin: God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth" (Act 17:26). Kinship brings duty, which is why the first murderer’s sneer, "Am I my brother’s keeper?" (Gen 4:9), is answered by the whole Bible with a yes. Abel’s blood cried from the ground against his brother; but the blood of Jesus, "the blood of sprinkling," "speaketh better things than that of Abel" (Heb 12:24) — it cries mercy, not vengeance. By that blood, strangers "who sometimes were far off are made nigh" (Eph 2:13), and the Son of God, who took our flesh and blood, "is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). That is the only blood-brotherhood that lasts. A father tells his son: call your friends what you like, but remember that every man you meet is your kin by Adam, and every believer is your brother by the blood of Christ — and treat the second kind as family, because the Lord does.

Webster 1828 Definition

Gen-Z slang (from blood, kinship; London MLE 1990s–2000s; US TikTok c. 2022–present) for bro or mate, often in mockery — a word Scripture fills with the one blood of all mankind and the better blood of Christ that makes believers brethren.

expand to see more

BLUD, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2022–present in the US; London MLE from the 2000s) Bro, mate, friend; a term of address. "You good, blud?"

US meme use, in the third person, mocking someone’s confidence: "blud thinks he can sing." London pairing: "wagwan, blud" (what’s going on).

Older senses a grandparent will know: blood for kin ("blood is thicker than water"); 1960s–70s Black American blood for a fellow Black man; in some US cities also a gang greeting, so context matters.

Webster (1828), root word blood: “BLOOD, noun 1. The fluid which circulates through the arteries and veins of the human body, and of other animals, which is essential to the preservation of life. This fluid is generally red. If the blood of an animal is not red, such animal is called exsanguious, or white-blooded; the blood being white, or white tinged with blue. 2.”

Decode for parents: mostly a jokey "bro"; in the "blud thinks" format it is a put-down, and the older gang overlay is worth knowing.

Key Scripture

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Gen 4:9 — "And the LORD said unto Cain, Where is Abel thy brother? And he said, I know not: Am I my brother's keeper?"

Heb 12:24 — "And to Jesus the mediator of the new covenant, and to the blood of sprinkling, that speaketh better things than that of Abel."

Eph 2:13 — "But now in Christ Jesus ye who sometimes were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ."

Heb 2:11 — "For both he that sanctifieth and they who are sanctified are all of one: for which cause he is not ashamed to call them brethren,"

Modern Corruption

Blud borrows the language of blood kinship for casual address and, in its American meme form, for mockery; Scripture keeps the kinship and binds it to the blood of Christ.

expand to see more

The word’s root is a true thing. Blood means family, and family means obligation. Cain tried to slip that obligation with a shrug (Gen 4:9), and the ground itself testified against him. Gangs have always borrowed the language of blood for the same reason — it binds — and both the London and the American histories of this word run near that world. In its American TikTok form, blud mostly mocks: "blud thinks he’s him." A word for kin used to belittle a brother is a small picture of Cain.

The gospel takes the word back. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God "hath made of one blood all nations of men" (Act 17:26) — every human is a relative. And Christ made a nearer kindred by His own blood: those far off are "made nigh by the blood of Christ" (Eph 2:13), and He "is not ashamed to call them brethren" (Heb 2:11). If the Son of God is not ashamed to call us brothers, a Christian boy can learn to use a word like blud without a sneer, and to mean by it something of what Christ means.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English blod (blood) → blood as kinship → 1960s Black American address blood → London MLE blud (1990s–2000s) → US TikTok c. 2022.
